item.title: Linkbase
item.description:
01.10.2026

  • Redesigning Source Control at Anthropic
    summary

    TL;DR: Anthropic’s source control team describes Scion, an in-house version control system that replaced git for its monorepo after merged changes grew from about 2,500 to over 30,000 per day between May and September 2026.

    • Scale problem: Main branch history is nearly 100 GB, a compressed working copy exceeds 25 GB, and CI runs about 25 million checkouts per day. Naive fetching would mean over 600 PB of git traffic daily.
    • Design: Clients are assumed always online. The server handles history, blame, commits, merges and rebases. Clients keep a bounded object cache and use sparse, virtualized checkouts.
    • Data model: Changesets in a write-ahead log list changed files with content-addressed blob pointers. Moving a ref is a compare-and-swap on one Spanner row. No packfiles, no full repo copy anywhere.
    • Architecture: A per-node scion-daemon talks to regional scion-cache servers, which talk to authoritative scion-server instances on Spanner and cloud storage. Cache hit rate is over 99% at each tier.
    • Results: About 200x smaller CPU and memory footprint than the git mirror fleet, checkouts about 100x faster, and about 25% CI CPU capacity freed. Seven people built Scion and the Antique code review tool in about five months.
    • Limits: Not a general git replacement. It only fits very large monorepos and forces migration of review, search and CI. Without a global merge lock, conflicts happen and Claude is used to fix them.

    Takeaway: Agent-scale commit rates break human-scale tooling first in source control and CI. Most teams cannot adopt Scion, but server-side commits, API-first queries and sparse checkouts are ideas to look for in git platforms.
